stories.title: Kenya discharges last Ebola patient in key milestone to being declared free of the virus
stories.summary: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October 2026 By Wycliffe Muia Reporting from Nairobi Published 9 minutes ago Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient - the seventh to recover from the virus - marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation, which now begins a 42-day countdown to officially being declared Ebola-free. It had confirmed its first ever case of Ebola early in October when a Kenyan businessman died within days of arriving in the capital, Nairobi. He had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing outbreak that began in May. His mother also subsequently died. Kenya's health minister said 135 identified contacts of the infected patients had also completed their 21 days in isolation. "Today with the discharge of the last patient we can confirm and tell the world that seven patients have recovered - and all contacts have completed their follow-up monitoring," Aden Duale said.

Wednesday's opening hearing was adjourned until 18 November after defence lawyers representing the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr requested a new judge. The UN has warned of "widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists". Attalah told the BBC that a recent crackdown was meant to "send a chilling message" to "the very few newsrooms that are left". She warned: "Everybody should be careful, everybody should be scared, everybody should be wondering if they are next." Set up 13 years ago, Mada Masr became Egypt's leading independent news site with Attalah as its editor-in-chief and co-founder.

US Africa Command deputy head Lt Gen John Brennan said Madagascar's strategic location in the Indian Ocean made it important to global trade. He warned against what he called the "Sahel model", which he said risked fuelling instability across the continent. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, all under military rule, have reduced ties with the Western partners and turned to Russia to support their fight against jihadist groups. Russia has expanded its co-operation with Madagascar since the army seized power in 2025, supplying weapons and military instructors. "We are concerned about Russia wanting to proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent," Brennan told reporters in an online briefing. stories.title: Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PGDc Prefer DW on Google European colonialism was marked by the — often extremely violent — exploitation of people and resources. [Pictured: Clearing of land by setting grass on fire during a German research expedition to Tendaguru in German East Africa, 1909–1913] Image: Archiv/Museum für Naturkunde Advertisement Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men." But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire, and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared, remains the subject of intense debate. This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust . Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history. 'Murder for the very purpose of murder': The industrialized mass murder carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau had no direct precedent in colonial history. [Pictured: Cans of Zyklon B gas, Auschwitz-Birkenau, German Nazi concentration and extermination camp in Poland] Image: Taiftin/Depositphotos/IMAGO "I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposed to be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case." "Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story. From colonial brutality to Nazi rule The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers.

stories.title: Africa's fight against fake news: Who decides what's true?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5P8sx Prefer DW on Google In junta-run countries like Burkina Faso, fact-checking initiatives like Fasocheck are under increased government scrutiny Image: Boureima Salouka/DW Advertisement Misinformation threatens democracy worldwide: An exaggerated WhatsApp message, a manipulated TikTok video or an apparent breaking news alert on Facebook can mislead people in Africa and beyond — particularly in the run-up to elections. As artificial intelligence is making it increasingly easy to manipulate images, voices and videos, more and more countries are trying to equip their populations with skills to identify and counter fake news . But are these efforts really about raising awareness, or are certain governments using this fight to control public opinion, silence dissident voices and misguide the populace — from both within and outside of these respective nations? Civil society groups fill gaps left by governments Journalism lecturer Dani Madrid-Morales at the University of Sheffield believes that African governments must significantly step up their efforts to combat sources of disinformation and misinformation. He told DW that "there are very few countries — if any — that are actually doing a good job" of beating the influence of fake news.

stories.summary: African Development Bank Approves $200 Million Regional Trade Finance Line of Credit Facility for Tdb to Support Trade Across Africa 9 November 2026 Content from a Premium Partner African Development Bank (Abidjan) The Board of Directors of the African Development Bank Group has approved a $200 million Trade Finance Line of Credit facility between the African Development Bank and Trade and Development Bank (TDB). The facility is expected to boost intra-Africa trade, promote regional integration, and contribute to the reduction of the trade finance gap in Africa, in line with implementation aspirations of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). Approved on 28 October, this facility will enable TDB to extend trade finance to clients across Africa. It is expected to catalyse more than $1 billion in trade transactions over its 3.5-year tenor due to the revolving nature of underlying transactions. Beneficiaries include financial institutions, corporates and small and medium-sized enterprises engaged in import and export activities whose growth has been constrained by inadequate liquidity.

stories.title: 'Devastating message' as ANC records worst-ever result in South Africa election
stories.summary: Image source, EPA Image caption, Voters cast their ballots at a polling station during South Africa's local government elections in Johannesburg By Ed Habershon Reporting from Johannesburg Published 8 November 2026 South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic". While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 31% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 65% 20 years ago. The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.

stories.title: The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Somalia has the longest coastline in mainland Africa By Fardowsa Hanshi BBC Somali Published 7 November 2026 As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital. Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture. Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes. "It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.

stories.title: Au large du Sénégal, au moins 34 personnes sont mortes dans le naufrage d'une pirogue de migrants
stories.summary: Publicité Au large du Sénégal, au moins 34 personnes sont mortes dans le naufrage d'une pirogue de migrants Au moins 34 personnes ont péri dans le naufrage d'une pirogue de migrants au large de Kébémer, dans le nord-ouest du Sénégal, selon les médias publics sénégalais et une ONG. Les recherches se poursuivent pour retrouver d'éventuels survivants. Publié le : 08/11/2026 - 13:26 Modifié le : 09/11/2026 - 07:20 4 min Temps de lecture Partager Par : FRANCE 24 La plage surnommée "l’aéroport", le point de départ utilisé par des migrants tentant de rejoindre l’Europe par la route de l’Atlantique, le 9 mars 2026 à Mbour, au Sénégal. © Patrick Meinhardt, AFP Le nombre de victimes continue d'augmenter. Le bilan du naufrage d'une pirogue de migrants au large de Kébémer, dans le nord-ouest du Sénégal , est passé de 21 à 34 morts, selon un nouveau décompte provisoire rapporté dimanche 8 novembre par les médias publics sénégalais et une ONG. Des milliers de personnes originaires d' Afrique de l'Ouest, en majorité des jeunes, tentent depuis des années de gagner clandestinement l' Europe en empruntant la route de l'Atlantique, principalement vers l'archipel espagnol des Canaries, à bord d'embarcations surchargées, souvent vétustes.

stories.title: A Makalé, capitale d’un Tigré retombé aux mains de l’armée éthiopienne, l’écho persistant de la guerre
stories.summary: La ville a été reprise par l’armée fédérale le 3 octobre. Chassés de leur fief historique, les rebelles tigréens se sont retranchés dans les zones montagneuses de la région. stories.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
stories.summary: Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill. Photograph: EPA View image in fullscreen Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill. Photograph: EPA Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history. The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes. Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

stories.title: Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Like many neighbouring countries, Guinea-Bissau waits until babies are six weeks old to vaccinate them against hepatitis B, while the WHO says it should be done at birth (file photo) By Basma El Atti Â and Â Makuochi Okafor ,Â BBC Africa Published 5 November 2026 A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was "unethical" and "neocolonial". The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines. Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy. The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns. Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.

stories.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK
stories.summary: The patient, whose identity was not disclosed, had been sent to DR Congo by a humanitarian organisation to help support the response to the outbreak. Photograph: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP View image in fullscreen The patient, whose identity was not disclosed, had been sent to DR Congo by a humanitarian organisation to help support the response to the outbreak. Photograph: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed. “A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola ,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.” The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters. A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.

stories.title: The young politicians with African roots making history in the US midterms
stories.summary: Figure caption, Watch: Abdul El-Sayed thanks supporters for backing 'unlikeliest of candidates' By Basma El Atti Published 4 November 2026 "JD [Vance], habibi (my love)". It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections. Abdul El-Sayed , 42, born to Egyptian immigrant parents, playfully addressed Vice-President JD Vance, who had campaigned against him but will now swear him into office in January as Michigan's new Senator. The US-born Democrat spent much of his campaign fending off attacks from conservative media and President Donald Trump, who accused him of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejected the allegations. "My name is Abdul Rahman Mohammed El-Sayed," he said in an Egyptian Arabic accent to the cheering crowd at his victory rally.

stories.title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
stories.summary: A voter casts their ballot in Lawley township, south of Johannesburg, South Africa. Photograph: Oupa Nkosi/Reuters View image in fullscreen A voter casts their ballot in Lawley township, south of Johannesburg, South Africa. Photograph: Oupa Nkosi/Reuters ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure. The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls showed it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections .
